newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels harden stand ahead of new crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels harden stand ahead of new crisis talks.

text.p: Peruvian Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's house for 102 days denied on Saturday that they had accepted asylum abroad and reiterated their demand that jailed comrades be freed.

Toughening their position ahead of an expected resumption of direct talks with the government next week, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels said reports of their likely acceptance of political asylum in Cuba were false.

"These and other declarations repeatedly made to the press are government lies which only seek to add to the confusion and hamper a political solution," said a statement issued on the MRTA's Internet web site.

Reinforcing the point, rebels inside the mansion scampered across the roof of the building before dawn to drape a banner from the rooftop saying, "We shall defend with our lives the freedom of our jailed (comrades)."
"For now, this is our response to what the government's been saying," one of the hostage-takers told Reuters by radio.

The rebel's Internet statement and the banner poured cold water on speculation in the local press that the two sides had reached a partial deal. According to the reports, the captors had accepted safe haven in Cuba and authorities agreed to free some but not all of the jailed rebels.
The release of 450 imprisoned MRTA members was the main demand made by the MRTA after rebels stormed the diplomatic residence on Dec. 17, taking hundreds of hostages.

Most of the hostages were released in the first weeks of the crisis. The MRTA still holds its most prized bargaining chips, including two cabinet ministers, generals, businessmen, President Alberto Fujimori's brother Pedro, the ambassadors of Bolivia and Japan, and two dozen Japanese nationals.
The MRTA's muscle flexing was the latest in a series of fluctuations in the negotiations, which moved back and forth all week between optimism and doubt.
On Friday, hours after Fujimori said things were looking up, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said in Tokyo: "I am not optimistic." He did not elaborate.

The hostages, who spent Christmas and New Year's at the residence, spent Good Friday eating traditional fish dishes and listening to messages from their families on the radio -- their only direct contact with the outside world.

"With great affection Nandito, we hope that in this Holy Week the Lord hears our prayers so that this moment passes soon," said one relative who, like others, used a nickname so as not to identify the hostage.
"I know that you have great strength," the message continued. "This Good Friday all our children are here. I love you. Take care of yourself. Goodbye my dear."
In the nearby port of Callao, thousands of Peruvians marched in an Easter procession devoted to the captives.
"In the name of God, when are you going to free our brothers -- the hostages?," Bishop Miguel Irizar, who presided over the Via Crucis (Way of the Cross) procession, asked the rebels.
Face-to-face talks between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa, broken off on March 12, were expected to resume on Monday or Tuesday.
Two of three guarantors mediating in the crisis met with MRTA leaders but made no comments afterward.
Peruvian officials, while saying an agreement was nearer, admit the main obstacle continues to be the demand for the release of imprisoned rebels.

In a separate statement, rebels expressed concern about the deteriorating health of women comrades on a hunger strike at Lima's Chorrillos prison, who they said were suffering from illnesses worsened by alleged torture and bad conditions.
A poll found that 84 percent of Peruvians favour improving jail conditions for those held on terrorism and treason convictions in exchange for the hostages' freedom.
The survey by local pollster Imasen also said 89 percent opposed freedom for jailed rebels and 75.5 percent felt the captors should leave Peru as part of a deal to end the crisis.
